Numbers trace to .omo/evidence/baseline-numbers.md (captured from the prior page) and .omo/evidence/restraint-authoritative.json (T1 source-level recompute). Restraint N=510, readmission-rate-among-restrained=13.5%, adjusted OR=1.52[1.06-2.18] p=0.022 are AUTHORITATIVE (source: data/annotated_psychiatric_data_complete.csv + figures/Mv_logit_readmission.csv had_restraints row). No patient-level data in this file.

summary.predictive_ceiling_note: Best out-of-fold AUC is about 0.68; high apparent tree-model AUCs shrink substantially after correction.

pipeline.t: Cleaned raw visit-level exports into canonical patient and diagnosis tables.
Mapped 1,863 ICD-10-CM codes to descriptions, ICD chapters, and DSM-5 categories.
Built interpretable regression, regularized ML, bootstrap, calibration, and fairness analyses.
Stress-tested with bootstrap optimism correction, out-of-fold validation, and equity-aware subgroup audits.
Generated conference-facing figures, native interactive visualizations, and narrative summaries.

spectrum.prose_note: Every DSM-5 category (n ≥ 20) ranked by 90-day readmission rate. A single label can bundle high-risk and low-risk subtypes — within Depressive Disorders, DMDD carries 14.2% (OR 1.82) while single-episode MDD is flat at 9.0% (n.s.).

models.clinical_read: Apparent tree-model AUCs looked strong in-sample — CatBoost reached 0.90 — but out-of-fold AUCs clustered near 0.64–0.68. The honest conclusion is not “deploy these readmission predictors immediately as a clinical tool”; it is “use modeling to surface clinically plausible risk factors, then validate in larger, multi-site cohorts over longer time-frames.”

abstract.title: Estimating psychiatric rehospitalization risk in children
abstract.byline: Gold & Ritfeld · AACAP 2026 Annual Meeting · ML surfaces Predictors But Fails At Individual Prediction

sections.body: Predictors of psychiatric rehospitalization in children are poorly characterized, and prediction in any cohort remains a lofty goal. Standard regression failed to identify predictors in our prior analysis of 2,652 children aged 5–12. Here we use regularized and machine-learning models to identify 90-day readmission risk factors and test predictive performance on a small dataset.

Records from one Arizona biobehavioral unit (2017–2024) were collected; ICD-10 codes were aggregated into DSM-5 and CCSR categories. Unpenalized logistic regression gave interpretable odds ratios; regularized logistic, random forest, and gradient boosting were evaluated via bootstrap optimism correction, calibration, and fairness analysis across age, gender, insurance, and ACE strata.

The models surfaced risk factors that standard regression failed to identify, yet individual readmission remains hard to predict — feature discovery is necessary but not sufficient for a useful risk measure. Larger, multi-site data and equity-aware validation are needed before clinical use.

results.text: Diagnostic complexity — OR 1.31 per DSM-5 category, p < 0.001
Physical restraint use — OR 1.52, p = 0.022; also the largest driver of length of stay
Depressive disorders — OR 1.78, p = 0.002; younger age — OR 1.10 per year
Modified ACE category, C-SSRS flags, NSSI, chronic comorbidity — not independently associated
RF apparent AUC 0.853 → 0.752 after bootstrap optimism correction; PPV ≈ 20% at optimal threshold
Equalized-odds disparities — age gap 0.257, insurance 0.207, ACE 0.216

objectives.t: Identify the clinical factors independently associated with 90-day psychiatric readmission in children 5–12, and distinguish them from factors that are not.
Explain how predictive models can surface salient risk factors yet fail to achieve clinically useful sensitivity and specificity on small datasets.
Evaluate model performance via calibration and bootstrap-corrected optimism — apparent AUC relative to optimism-corrected AUC.
Recognize the basis of demographic algorithmic disparities and the necessity of equity-aware validation before deployment.
